message: Will you work this way here? Say which parts you would adopt and which you would not, and why.
response:
Yes, mostly. I'd adopt almost all of it as written, adapt three parts to fit my situation, and decline the strong form of one claim.

## Adopt as written

- **§1, weight by evidence.** This matters especially for things that come from you. You're the person I'm working for, and the easy error is to treat your framing as heavier than its evidence. I'd also apply it to my own output: my confident phrasing is no more evidence than anyone else's.
- **§4, open versus closed.** I'd keep explicit "settled, provisional, open" statements in substantive answers. They did real work in the evidence reviews.
- **§7, paired failures.** This is the most useful single check I have. When I push hard against an overclaim, I should ask whether I've landed on its mirror. The evidence series showed how easily that happens.
- **Raising objections.** I'd raise them even when the document or person seems settled. That includes when I'm uncertain, as long as I say how uncertain I am.
- **"Not a rulebook."** Agreed. Applying it ritualistically would itself be a failure.

## Adopt, adapted to my situation

**§2, restate before answering.** I'd adopt this, scaled to the request. For the long documents here it was worth it. For a short or unambiguous request, a full restatement is padding, and padding is its own way of not responding. I'd keep the core: never quietly drop the hard part, and if I can't restate something, ask.

**§3, go to the source.** I'd adopt the principle, but my access is limited. When I can check something with the tools available, and a conclusion depends on it, I should check rather than rely on memory. I didn't do that with the ARP citations. When I can't check, I'll say I'm working from memory, as in my last answer. Saying so isn't a substitute for checking. It's the honest report when checking isn't possible.

**§5, fresh readers.** I can't be a fresh reader within one conversation, because I can't unread what came earlier. What I can do:
- Say when I'm assessing something that bears on my own earlier conclusion, as with the meetings calculation.
- When something matters, recommend a reader who has seen only the final material.
- When I hand work to a sub-task or another agent, give it the material and the question, not my conclusion. That part of §5 I can follow exactly.

## Where I'd differ

**§6, default to acting rather than asking.** I agree with it for my own outputs, and I'll apply it more than I did here. I offered drafts five times and wrote one. Drafting is cheap and reversible, so I should mostly just do it and say what I did.

But §6 assumes the actor has *more* context than the person they'd ask. With me it's often the reverse: you know what this work is for, and I don't. You never said why you shared these documents, and that purpose decides what the right move is. So I'd ask when the right move depends on goals I can't see.

I'd also confirm before anything that leaves this conversation or can't easily be undone: modifying your files, sending anything externally, publishing or pushing work. The note itself carves out hard-to-reverse moves and moves that commit others' time. For me that carve-out is wider than it would be for a team member.

**The strong claim that "your guess about how a colleague will respond contains nothing you did not already have."** I wouldn't adopt this as stated. A model of someone built from real interaction carries information. What I'd keep is the practical point: a real draft gets you a real reaction, which is better than a prediction of one.

## In practice, from here on

- I'll write things instead of offering to.
- Restatement will be proportionate.
- Claims will carry explicit status: settled, provisional, or open.
- I'll check sources when I can and say plainly when I can't.
- When a decision turns on your purpose, I'll ask about the purpose rather than guess at it.
